content: Lapsana is a genus of flowering plants within the family Asteraceae, and it contains only one species, Lapsana communis, commonly known as Nipplewort. This plant is native to Europe and northern Asia. It can grow up to 2 meters in height and is characterized by hairy stems and clear sap, which is not milky. The leaves of Lapsana communis are arranged spirally. The larger leaves located at the base of the flowering stem are often pinnate, featuring a large oval terminal leaflet and one to four smaller side leaflets. In contrast, the smaller leaves higher up on the stem are simple and oval in shape. All leaves have toothed margins. The flowers of Lapsana communis are yellow and are produced in capitula that measure 1–2 cm in diameter. These capitula are numerous and form loose clusters at the top of the stem. There are six recognized subspecies of Lapsana communis: Lapsana communis subsp. communis: Found in most of Europe, excluding the southeast. It is an annual plant. Lapsana communis subsp. adenophora (Boiss. f.): Found in southeastern Europe. Lapsana communis subsp. alpina (Boiss. Sell.): Found in Crimea. Lapsana communis subsp. grandiflora (M. Bieb. Sell.): Found in southwest Asia. Lapsana communis subsp. intermedia (M. Bieb.) Hayek: Found in southwest Asia and southeastern Europe. It is a perennial plant. Lapsana communis subsp. pisidica (Boiss. & Heldr. f.): Found in Greece. Historically, other species were included in the genus Lapsana, but these are now classified under the genera Crepis and Lapsanastrum. Cultivation and Uses The young leaves of Lapsana communis are edible and can be consumed raw in salads or cooked in a manner similar to spinach. The scientific name Lapsana originates from an edible herb described by Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar. The English name Nipplewort is derived from the appearance of its closed flower buds, which resemble nipples. Due to this resemblance, and following the doctrine of signatures, it was historically used as a treatment for breast ulcers. Outside its native range, Lapsana communis has become naturalized in many regions worldwide. In some areas, it is considered an invasive species, including in Australia, Chile, New Zealand, and most of North America.
